items.title: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
items.summary: The Japanese Space Agency has launched the Mars Moons Exploration mission to collect and return 10g of dust from the Martian moon Phobos. This ambitious project aims to determine the origin of Mars's moons by analyzing pristine samples in Earth-based laboratories.

brief.what: The Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) spacecraft has launched from Japan to study Phobos and Deimos, with the goal of returning 10g of surface material to Earth. The mission involves deploying a rover to scout landing sites before the main craft collects samples for return in 2031.
brief.who: The Japanese Space Agency (JAXA) leads the mission, with international scientific collaboration from institutions including the Natural History Museum and Leicester University.
brief.context: Scientists currently debate whether Phobos and Deimos formed from debris following a massive impact on Mars or if they are captured asteroids. Previous efforts to return Martian samples, such as the NASA/ESA Mars Sample Return mission, have faced significant funding hurdles.
brief.why: Researchers seek to analyze the mineral composition of the samples to definitively identify the moons' origins. Prof Sara Russell notes that the samples may also contain grains from Mars itself, providing direct data on the planet's history.
brief.next: The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027, with the sample capsule expected to land in South Australia in 2031.

items.author: By Bob Berwyn

brief.what: A study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reveals that deep-sea animal populations in the Gulf of Mexico declined by 60 to 85 percent following the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster. The article suggests that Congress should intervene to cancel the increase or reform the calculation method to improve fiscal sustainability.

also.author: Rachel Greszler
also.title: Social Security’s Cost-of-Living Adjustment Will Soon Become a Cost-of-Insolvency Adjustment
also.note: National Review frames the adjustment as a direct contributor to the program's insolvency rather than focusing on the fairness of the payout.

brief.what: Social Security trustees are set to implement a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for retirees, despite the program facing long-term insolvency. The author argues this increase is fiscally irresponsible and suggests that Congress should either cancel the adjustment or switch to a broader inflation index to reduce the program's shortfall.
brief.who: The Social Security trustees, who manage the program, and Congress, which has the authority to intervene in benefit calculations.
brief.context: Social Security is currently trending toward insolvency because benefit payouts exceed tax collections. The program uses the CPI-W index to calculate annual adjustments, which critics argue is a narrow measure of inflation that does not accurately reflect the cost of living for all Americans.
brief.why: The author contends that the COLA is unfair to workers whose wages have not kept pace with inflation and that the current system disproportionately benefits wealthy retirees. The article claims that changing the calculation to the CPI-U index could address 12% of the program's long-term funding gap.

items.title: What to Know About the Obscure Trust Looming Over Anthropic’s IPO
items.author: Theo Francis
items.summary: Anthropic has disclosed limited information regarding a five-person trust that holds significant authority over its board and strategic decision-making. This governance structure remains a focal point as the company prepares for a potential initial public offering.

brief.what: Anthropic is facing scrutiny over a five-person trust that possesses the power to influence board composition and block major corporate actions. The company has provided minimal transparency regarding the specific dynamics and operational mechanics of this governing body.
brief.who: Anthropic, an artificial intelligence company, is the primary actor involved in this governance arrangement.
brief.context: The company is currently navigating the complexities of corporate governance as it moves toward a potential initial public offering.
brief.why: The trust was established to shape the board and control major moves, though the company has shared few details on how these dynamics function.

items.title: Opinion | The Northeast Climate Revolt
items.author: The Editorial Board
items.summary: Rising utility costs driven by anti-fossil fuel policies are creating political challenges for Democrats in the Northeast. The issue has become a focal point for the party as they navigate an election year.

brief.what: Anti-fossil fuel policies in the Northeast have led to increased utility bills for residents. This economic pressure is forcing Democratic politicians to play defense during the current election cycle.
brief.who: Democratic politicians in the Northeast are the primary actors facing political pressure due to these energy policies.
brief.context: The region is experiencing a shift in energy policy that directly impacts the cost of living for constituents, creating a vulnerability for incumbents.
brief.why: According to the Wall Street Journal, the policies are being challenged because they have resulted in higher utility costs, which has become a liability for Democrats in an election year.

items.title: Climate scientists face deluge of public-records requests about fossil-fuel studies
items.author: James Dinneen
items.summary: Climate scientists are facing a surge in public-records requests from groups linked to the energy industry, which researchers believe are intended to discredit climate attribution science. These legal demands target correspondence related to studies that link fossil-fuel emissions to specific environmental damages.

brief.what: Climate scientists in the U.S. are experiencing a significant increase in public-records requests, with at least 30 identified since 2024 across 13 universities. These requests, often filed by groups with ties to the energy industry, seek correspondence related to climate attribution research used in litigation against industrial emitters.
brief.who: The main actors include climate scientists, the Patriots Foundation, Government Accountability and Oversight, and the Climate Science Legal Defense Fund.
brief.context: Climate attribution science, which estimates the link between human-caused emissions and specific extreme weather events, has become increasingly central to legal cases seeking to hold fossil-fuel companies responsible for climate-related damages.
brief.why: Researchers suggest the requests are an effort to fish for perceived conflicts of interest to discredit their findings and dissuade further work. Conversely, groups like Government Accountability and Oversight argue that if scientists engage in lobbying, the public has a right to review their correspondence under transparency laws.
